cards.title: The four-step Google Ads pipeline: retrieval, elimination, ranking, auction
cards.summary: Understanding Google's internal ad-serving sequence explains why relevance, not budget, drives placement.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why Shopping or Search ads aren't showing, or deciding what to optimize first when a product campaign underperforms.
steps: Map your current campaigns against the four stages: retrieval (Google scans your landing page, titles, descriptions, images, price point, keywords, demographics to decide relevance), elimination (irrelevant or negative-scoring ads are discarded), ranking (surviving ads ordered by ad score), auction (CPC set by the buyer's intent and your relevance).
For retrieval optimization, treat your entire feed as your targeting data — fix weak images, vague titles, mismatched price points and missing attributes, since Google reads all of them.

For elimination, focus on what the source calls the ad score formula (DOJ-disclosed): bid x predicted click-through rate, minus a penalty variable (beta) reflecting user experience and landing page quality. Ads scoring negative are removed from the ranking entirely.
For ranking, once bid is automated and beta is low, the remaining lever is predicted CTR: make assets relevant to the searcher's history and current query.
Recognize the auction is pay-per-click, not pay-per-impression, so a weak click means real money spent without a purchase — relevant copy protects CPC.
Explain the audience-facing rationale to stakeholders: relevance gets you into the auction, keeps you from elimination, lifts your rank, and earns cheaper intent-rich clicks.
caveats: The ad score formula is attributed to DOJ disclosure in the source; treat the exact structure as the source's interpretation rather than verified Google documentation.
Position-click-share figures (40% for position one) come from the source's cited chart and should be validated against current SERP behavior before planning around them.

cards.title: Surface area scaling: duplicate products across pricing tiers to own the search page
cards.summary: Multiply one winning product into multiple listings differentiated by price tier so you occupy several ad slots at once.
cards.use_when: Product selection, merchandising and campaign structure decisions when a single hero SKU is already profitable and you want to grow without simply raising budget.
steps: Start with one product and one winning angle that is already converting.
Instead of only increasing budget on the original listing, duplicate the product several times (the source cites five to six duplicates).
For each duplicate, shift one axis: price tier (budget, standard, discount, premium, luxury), and adjust titles/images to match so each listing reads as a distinct offer rather than a clone.

Verify the newly created variants don't cannibalize the original: the source reports seeing little cannibalization between variants, but track blended CPC and conversion by variant before adding more.
Use the duplicated listings to compete for price-qualified queries (e.g. 'under $30' vs 'under $100') that a single mid-price listing would never enter.
Rebalance budget across variants based on which price tier is generating the better CPA/ROAS, not simply on the highest-volume variant.
caveats: The source's example of an operator appearing in six of seven slots is an anecdote from that operator's account, not a guaranteed outcome.
Maintaining many near-duplicate listings costs time in feed hygiene, price/stock sync and review — plan for the operational load.

cards.title: Differentiate duplicate listings with image angles matched to customer avatars
cards.summary: Instead of one product shot per SKU, create lifestyle/angle variants so each listing speaks to a different buyer persona.
cards.use_when: PDP/landing page and Shopping feed creative decisions when a single image set makes every product look like everyone else's.
steps: Take one product and separate images on a white background (the source claims this is what most competitors do) and ask which customer situations the product serves.
Create 2–4 variant images per product, each mapped to a distinct use case or avatar, e.g. leisure wear, active wear, corporate.
Match the visual context (setting, model, styling) to the persona's likely search intent so the shopper can see themselves using the product.

Note the source's claim that Google reads image content and demographics — if your images feature college students, Google may bias delivery toward them, so align avatar imagery with the audience you actually want.
Run duplicate listings with distinct image sets side by side to see whether the variant attracts a different click/order profile before expanding further.
Assign each variant a clear internal name matching the avatar so the merchandising team knows which listing serves whom.
caveats: Sources's avatar-image claim is the operator's interpretation of how Google infers audience from feed imagery, not documented Google behavior.
Producing genuine lifestyle variants per avatar is more expensive than editing one photo; only do this once the underlying product-converts.

cards.title: Write titles for the algorithm, not for the shopper
cards.summary: Keyword-stuff Google Ads titles/products using a consistent structure so each listing qualifies for many more queries.
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting Shopping feed titles, Search ad headlines, or PDP titles for paid traffic.
steps: Build titles on this structure, per the source: primary adjective, then product, then who it's for, USP, use cases, then specifics.

Compare broad vs narrow: 'heated jacket' competes on roughly two keyword concepts; 'heated jacket for men, USB rechargeable, temperature control for hiking/skiing/outdoor work, water resistant black' enters numerous keyword pools simultaneously.
Mine additional keywords in Google Ads Keyword Planner by entering the core product term, setting the target country, and exporting the returned search terms.
Feed the exported keyword list plus the title template into your preferred AI writing tool (the source uses Claude) to generate title variants in bulk.
Fill the description field too: use two paragraphs of natural copy that include use-case and person-specific keywords (winter, hunting, construction, poor circulation).
Keep the same core keyword structure across duplicate listings so the algorithm consistently recognizes each variant's relevance category.
caveats: Over-stuffing can harm brand perception and may violate feed quality guidelines; the source's aggressive approach assumes paid-only traffic.
Keywords must reflect what the product genuinely is — misleading titles risk negative beta (quality penalty) and refunds.

cards.title: Set up a lean Performance Max campaign limited to Search and Shopping
cards.summary: Strip out Gmail, Display, Maps, Discover and YouTube placements in PMax to concentrate budget on high-intent surfaces.
cards.use_when: Campaign setup for an ecommerce account launching its main Google campaign, or auditing an existing PMax that is spending on low-intent placements.
steps: Create campaign without guidance, choose Performance Max, set the account goal to purchases, and select the Google Merchant Center feed.
Leave the bidding/target fields blank at first (do not set tROAS on a new account).
Set locations to presence, not presence-or-interest — the source says the default presence-or-interest wastes budget on people unlikely to buy.
Turn off TV screens under devices.
On the asset page, leave all headlines, YouTube creatives and email assets blank; keep only products selected.
Disable text, image and video enhancement so the system does not auto-expand into YouTube, Gmail or Display placements.
If the platform errors on publishing the empty asset group, create the asset group fully, publish, duplicate it, leave the duplicate blank, then pause the original — per the source's workaround.
Ignore the ad strength score; the source reports it is always 'poor' when running PMax this way and still performs.
caveats: Interface fields and names change; verify against the current Google Ads UI before instructing a media buyer to follow this exactly.
Single-campaign consolidation is the source's opinion — sometimes brand and standard shopping campaigns still need to be layered.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Don't set a tROAS target before the account has conversion history
cards.summary: Premature tROAS targets throttle scaling; the source waits months before adding one.
cards.use_when: Deciding when to apply target ROAS to a Performance Max or Shopping campaign on a new or growing ecommerce account.
steps: Leave tROAS blank for the first roughly three months while you let PMax optimise against conversion data.
Wait until you see a plateau or efficiency drop before adding a target.
When adding a target, remember Google tROAS is the revenue target per ad dollar: 300% means you want $3 of revenue per $1 spent.
For campaigns that are already highly profitable, consider not adding a target at all — the source scaled a campaign to ~$500K spend without one to avoid limiting it.
If budget reaches roughly $20K–$30K/day and every incremental dollar returns less, layer in a standard shopping campaign rather than pushing budget higher on the same PMax campaign.
caveats: All dollar and timeframe figures are the source's operational heuristics from its own accounts, not benchmarks; profitability is store-specific.
Some accounts may be forced to set a target by the platform — check current requirements.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Consolidate campaigns instead of segmenting by product line
cards.summary: Contrary to popular advice to run many separated campaigns, the source argues one consolidated campaign outperforms segmented structures in ecommerce.
cards.use_when: Campaign architecture decisions when deciding how many Google campaigns to run per product category.
steps: Audit the current account and count campaigns; the source's stated position is that consolidation beats segmentation.
Aim to run as few campaigns as possible — ideally one dominant performer — rather than splitting by niche, product line or avatar.
Allow exceptions where structure genuinely differs: brand search, standard shopping and PMax may all need to coexist.
When one campaign is hitting diminishing returns, layer a second campaign underneath rather than fragmenting the original.
Review conversion and cost data by campaign monthly to confirm the consolidated structure is still the most efficient arrangement.
caveats: This is a source-specific opinion that runs against common practitioner guidance — segment structure can be required in accounts with very different margin structures or regions.
Rigid consolidation can hide underperforming SKUs; keep SKU-level reporting regardless of campaign structure.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Work the learning phase: 30 conversions in 30 days is the baseline, not a cap
cards.summary: Google's stated learning phase threshold is 30 conversions in 30 days, but aligned feeds can exit faster.
cards.use_when: Planning launch expectations and diagnosing persistent under-delivery after a new campaign or new ad account launch.
steps: Understand Google's definition per the source: 30 conversions within a 30-day window (roughly one conversion/day) exits the learning phase.
If the whole system is aligned — titles, descriptions, images, price, product selection — the source reports campaigns exiting learning in roughly the first week.
For new accounts, expect early instability: the source describes a typical trend of shaky first days, first order around day two or three, then multiple orders per day once Google has signal.
If a campaign stays in learning indefinitely, audit relevance alignment before increasing budget; poor alignment keeps Google from gathering usable customer data.
Reinforce wins by continuing to accumulate and double down on conversion data — the more conversions Google sees, the better its targeting.
Treat the 30-in-30 heuristic as a floor for accounts that are otherwise misaligned, not as a target to aim for.
caveats: The 30-in-30 figure is Google's stated definition per the source, and conversion counting rules vary by conversion action; verify current thresholds.
Faster exits reported by the source are from its own accounts and should not be promised.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Weekly optimisation cadence: tROAS, budget, negative keywords, product pruning
cards.summary: A tight weekly Google Ads review cycle beats constant tinkering; the source changes only a few levers each week.
cards.use_when: Setting up an ecommerce account's recurring Google Ads management routine.
steps: Schedule a fixed weekly review (the source uses Sundays) and in most weeks only touch three things: tROAS, budget, or prune keywords/products.
Pull the campaign report and identify products getting the most clicks and keywords driving the most clicks — these are the winners to protect.
Identify products selling poorly and keywords wasting spend, then remove them.
Use early-data reviews: even at ~$100 spend you can see which products and keywords attract clicks.
When making the change, prefer one lever at a time so you can attribute the effect; the source typically changes only one of tROAS, budget or pruning per week.
Track the long-term trend line weekly rather than intraday — Google's returns are historically steadier across weeks than social platforms'.
caveats: No performance guarantees; the weekly cadence is the source's operating habit, not a proven optimal formula.
Over-frequent pruning can remove keywords still in an early learning stage — judge with enough impression/click data.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Use Google's intent-by-relevance CPC model to gauge paid search economics
cards.summary: Google's modern CPC is described by the source as the customer's purchasing intent multiplied by the advertiser's relevance.
cards.use_when: Evaluating keyword/bid economics and deciding whether a mid-relevance advertiser should compete on a high-intent query.
steps: Think of each searcher in tiers of purchase intent (the source illustrates a 1x lightly-interested buyer up to a ~3x frequent ad buyer).
Think of each ad in tiers of relevance to the query (the most relevant seller gets the lowest multiplier, an irrelevant one a higher multiplier).
Multiply the two: the most relevant advertiser attracts the highest-intent buyer at a favourable CPC, while a less relevant advertiser pays far more for the same click.
Use this to justify why investing in relevance (titles, images, price tier) reduces effective CPCs and improves downstream conversion rate and average order value.
Before bidding aggressively on a broad term, confirm your listing genuinely matches the buyer's stated need — otherwise you are the advertiser paying the high multiplier.
Remember Google charges per click (not per impression like Facebook), so a poorly relevant click is pure loss — relevant copy and matching landing pages protect spend.
caveats: The specific multipliers (1x–3x, 1x–5x) are the source's illustrative numbers, not a published Google formula.
Relevance-driven CPC improvement compounds slowly and requires consistent feed quality.

cards.title: Add a branded search campaign to defend your brand term cheaply
cards.summary: A separate brand campaign ensures your store appears first when shoppers search your name.
cards.use_when: Defensive campaign setup for an established ecommerce brand seeing competitors or review sites outrank its own name in search.
steps: Confirm your brand name has meaningful search volume before building the campaign.
Set up a dedicated branded search campaign so that when a customer types your brand, your listing appears above competitors and review sites.
The source reports little cannibalisation between a brand campaign and general PMax spend and treats it as a low-cost defensive layer.
Monitor the brand campaign separately to confirm real incremental value rather than capturing clicks you would have won organically.
Keep expectations modest relative to PMax — the source characterises it as a small add-on that handles a fraction of revenue.
caveats: Attribution between brand search and organic remains difficult; ensure you are not paying for conversions you would get anyway.
Brand keywords have different CPC dynamics than generic terms.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Treat beta (experience penalty) as the long-term ranking lever
cards.summary: The source's ad score formula subtracts a penalty for poor post-click experience, and that penalty decreases with persistent quality and conversion history.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest alongside acquisition — site speed, delivery reliability, customer experience — to lower paid search costs over time.
steps: Recognise that beta penalises slow landing pages, poor store experience and non-delivery; it lowers ad score and directly worsens eligibility and rank.
Treat reducing beta as a daily compounding effort: keep landing pages fast and accurate, ship orders on time, and avoid scam-adjacent practices.
Earn trust through accumulated conversions and good customer experiences, which the source says lowers beta and, in turn, reduces clicks costs and lifts ranking.

Look at long-term trends: the source argues Google is a long-horizon platform (returns sustained over 2–5 years) compared with the up/down volatility of social platforms, provided the fundamentals remain aligned.
Keep the same store/account running to build trust equity, rather than constantly starting fresh accounts.
Prioritise relevance-hitting work (titles, images, pricing) for quick PCTR gains while beta improves slowly through consistent operations.
caveats: The beta variable and its long-term effect are the source's framing, not Google-published mechanics; treat directionally.
The 2–5 year ROI claim is anecdotal to the source's accounts.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Build a broad keyword pool with Keyword Planner before writing feed copy
cards.summary: Mine real search terms in Keyword Planner and feed them into title/description templates to widen your query coverage.
cards.use_when: Paid search or Shopping feed title and description creation, and expansion of a keyword strategy.
steps: Open Keyword Planner (free) from within Google Ads and enter the core product term.
Set the target country and run results to see the actual related search terms people use (e.g. for 'heated jacket': electric jacket, self-heating jacket, heated coat, heated hunting clothes).
Export the keyword list, then combine it with your structured title template (adjective, product, audience, USP, use cases, specifics).
Generate titles and two-paragraph descriptions in bulk with an AI writing tool, sitting every returned keyword into the relevant slot.
Load the generated titles/descriptions into the feed or campaign asset, checking that each title still reads as coherent customer-facing copy.
Repeat for each surface-area listing variant so its keyword pool reflects its specific price tier and avatar.
caveats: The Keyword Planner surface and export workflow change periodically; verify current UI steps.
Keyword-stuffed description copy can look spammy in customer-facing storefronts; keep the aggressive version for ad/feed fields.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Prefer PVMs consolidations before adding new campaign types
cards.summary: Before introducing a new campaign type, confirm your current single campaign has genuinely plateaued.
cards.use_when: Scaling an ecommerce ad account when tempted to add campaign types to solve a performance plateau.
steps: Evaluate whether you have hit diminishing returns on the existing campaign — the source's trigger is often a budget around $20K–$30K/day where marginal return falls.
When that happens, layer a standard shopping campaign beneath the PMax rather than spreading budget across many new campaign types.
Keep brand search as a separate small layer for defensive coverage.
Only introduce additional campaign types when they address a specific structural need (brand, control over CPC via standard shopping) rather than a general wish for more reach.
If you do scale further, consider asset groups and tROAS adjustments before launching entirely new campaign categories.
Keep campaign count low: the source structured accounts so one campaign produced ~99% of revenue.
caveats: Thresholds cited are the source's own operating observations and vary by category and margin.
This consolidation bias can conflict with the needs of large accounts requiring geo or margin-based segmentation.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Interview alignment: relevance across feed, landing page and price point
cards.summary: The algorithm scans the entire store surface as targeting data, so misaligned listings dilute delivery.
cards.use_when: Landing page and feed QA when diagnosing declining impressions, rising CPCs or low volume of conversions after a period of stability.
steps: Audit every attribute Google can read: titles, descriptions, images, price point, keywords, demographics implied by imagery.
For each duplication/surface-area variant, confirm the price, imagery and copy actually correspond to the buyer segment the listing is meant to attract.
For a variant pitched at a budget buyer, show budget-relevant imagery and price transparently on the landing page so post-click experience matches the ad.
Check landing page load speed — the source attributes beta penalties partly to slow pages.
Align ad copy language (use cases, audience) with the actual PDP copy so the searcher's expectation is met.
Fix the top few high-traffic listings first and measure whether CPC and CTR improve before touching the long tail.
caveats: The claim that Google scans landing-page speed into a beta penalty is the source's interpretation and should be considered directionally, not as verified mechanics.
Improvements compound over weeks; don't judge a listing change from a single day of data.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx

cards.title: Aim for high page position and read the clicks-per-position trade-off
cards.summary: Higher ranked positions capture disproportionately more click share, so ranking work is fundamentally a demand-capture play.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations for a Google campaign and prioritising rank/impression-share work over superficial creative prettiness.
steps: Use the source's cited click-share gradient (roughly 40% position one, ~20% position two, ~10% position three, ~7% position four) as a directional illustration of why rank matters.
Recognise that for a given query you are not up against thousands of advertisers, only the handful of listings competing for those slots.
Prioritise relevance work (feed titles, images, price tiers) which the source says raises PCTR, ad score and therefore rank.
Combine rank work with surface-area duplication so that even the lower slots you occupy are yours, multiplying the share you capture.
Track impression share and position over time to see whether the relevance changes actually shifted you upward.
caveats: The click-share percentages are the source's cited chart values and vary by query type, device and SERP layout today; validate with your own data.
Position one does not guarantee high conversion rate — poorly matched searchers may click and bounce.
cards.source_name: ENTIRE google ads algorithm explained in 24 mins.docx
